article_title: The Devil is in the Details: AI Agents, Ghost Students, and the Crisis of Verified Presence in an Agentic AI World
citation: Aras Bozkurt, Helen Crompton, & Caroline Fell Kurban. (2026). The Devil is in the Det[ai]ls: AI Agents, Ghost Students, and the Crisis of Verified Presence in an Agentic AI World. Open Praxis, 18(1), 1–12. https://doi.org/10.55982/openpraxis.18.1.1145
title: The ghost student: agentic AI as mind plus AI browser as body producing a verification gap in digital education
description: The article's organizing framework describes the ghost student as a digital surrogate created by coupling Large Language Models (the mind) with agentic AI browsers (the body). Agentic AI is defined as systems designed to operate autonomously, adapt dynamically, and execute multi-step processes to achieve predefined goals with minimal human intervention, and the browser supplies embodied actions such as clicking, scrolling, and submitting work. The result is a verification gap: a digital entity that satisfies every metric of success while the human learner remains entirely disengaged, making the learner's presence optional and eroding credential trust.
requirements: Institutional systems that infer learning from logged-in activity and output-based submissions, which the surrogate can satisfy without a human present
constraints: The framework addresses agentic AI browsers acting with valid authenticated credentials; it is an argument-based editorial account, not an empirically tested model
target_learners: open, online and distance education learners
examples: The editorial describes AI browsers logging into an LMS with valid credentials, navigating modules, watching videos, responding to quizzes, and submitting assignments without further human input
key_sources: Aras Bozkurt, Helen Crompton, & Caroline Fell Kurban. (2026). The Devil is in the Det[ai]ls: AI Agents, Ghost Students, and the Crisis of Verified Presence in an Agentic AI World. Open Praxis, 18(1), 1–12. https://doi.org/10.55982/openpraxis.18.1.1145

article_title: Supporting Literacy Assessment in West Africa: Using State-of-the-Art Speech Models to Assess Oral Reading Fluency
citation: Henkel, O., Horne-Robinson, H., Hills, L., Roberts, B., & McGrane, J. (2025). Supporting Literacy Assessment in West Africa: Using State-of-the-Art Speech Models to Assess Oral Reading Fluency. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00435-9
title: Ghana ORF Dataset: publicly available oral reading fluency recordings from Ghanaian students
description: The University of Oxford & Rising Academies Ghanaian Student Oral Reading Fluency Dataset contains the results from ORF tasks administered in a Ghanaian school network, including original passages, audio recordings of students reading, and high-quality human transcriptions. The authors state it addresses a gap because "there are no publicly available datasets of children's voices speaking English that (a) focus on students' oral reading rather than speaking and (b) are from countries other than the United States, Canada, or the United Kingdom." Passages came from PrePIRLS, designed for LMICs.
requirements: Human transcriptions were produced by careful relistening, estimated at approximately 5 min per story, to faithfully preserve added or repeated words
constraints: Recordings come from students of one school network on the peri-urban periphery of Accra, so the sample is regionally specific
target_learners: Students aged 9-18 in Ghana, grades spanning primary to secondary
examples: 130 readers (of 162 screened, 32 nonreaders) read short passages aloud; 239 recordings total; 35 of 130 students (15%) reported speaking English at home
key_sources: Henkel, O., Horne-Robinson, H., Hills, L., Roberts, B., & McGrane, J. (2025). Supporting Literacy Assessment in West Africa: Using State-of-the-Art Speech Models to Assess Oral Reading Fluency. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00435-9

article_title: Ghana Heart Initiative Training for Cardiac Arrest Management Among Health Care Professionals: Outcomes Evaluation Study (2019-2024).
citation: Doku A, Tuglo LS, Osuoji C, Edzeame J, Broni M, Mainoo DD, Acquah AE, Honny K, Peters RJG, Agyemang C. (2025). Ghana Heart Initiative Training for Cardiac Arrest Management Among Health Care Professionals: Outcomes Evaluation Study (2019-2024). JMIR Formative Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/75536
title: Ghana Heart Initiative BLS and ACLS training and assessment package based on AHA 2018 and 2020 guidelines
description: A training and assessment package delivered by Code Red, an AHA-certified provider, consisting of 1-day BLS and 3-day ACLS courses using "lectures with PowerPoint presentations, video materials, practical demonstrations, and hands-on exercises." Course materials were provided "at least 4 weeks prior to the training for preparation." Assessment used a standardized 20-item questionnaire (10 BLS, 10 ACLS) plus CPR skills drills immediately after training, with scores ≥90% classified as adequate. The authors state it "created a standard for BLS and ACLS training and assessment that could be used in Ghana and other countries."
requirements: course guide distributed at least 4 weeks before training for preparation
constraints: immediate post-training assessment may not reflect real-world emergency performance and may introduce social desirability bias (authors' stated limitation)
target_learners: health care professionals in Ghana (physician assistants, nurses, house officers, medical officers, senior medical officers, specialists, trainee specialists)
target_learning_goals: BLS and ACLS knowledge and skills for cardiac arrest and cardiovascular emergency management
examples: 541 professionals trained in BLS and 302 in ACLS across 8 of Ghana's 16 regions from 2019 to 2024, sampled across 44 primary, secondary, and tertiary public and quasi-governmental facilities.
key_sources: Doku A, Tuglo LS, Osuoji C, Edzeame J, Broni M, Mainoo DD, Acquah AE, Honny K, Peters RJG, Agyemang C. (2025). Ghana Heart Initiative Training for Cardiac Arrest Management Among Health Care Professionals: Outcomes Evaluation Study (2019-2024). JMIR Formative Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/75536
